title: Electrolytes
lead: Some substances give ions when they dissolve in water, and the ions are what let a solution conduct electricity. Solutes differ in how fully they form ions, from ionic solids that come apart in water to covalent compounds that must react with it, and a conductivity test tells strong electrolytes, weak electrolytes and nonelectrolytes apart.
objectives: Define and give examples of electrolytes
Distinguish between the physical and chemical changes that accompany dissolution of ionic and covalent electrolytes
Relate electrolyte strength to solute-solvent attractive forces
summary_html: Substances that dissolve in water to yield ions are called electrolytes. Electrolytes may be covalent compounds that chemically react with water to produce ions (for example, acids and bases), or they may be ionic compounds that dissociate to yield their constituent cations and anions, when dissolved. Dissolution of an ionic compound is facilitated by ion-dipole attractions between the ions of the compound and the polar water molecules. Soluble ionic substances and strong acids ionize completely and are strong electrolytes, while weak acids and bases ionize to only a small extent and are weak electrolytes. Nonelectrolytes are substances that do not produce ions when dissolved in water.

exercises.prompt: Explain why the ions Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> are strongly solvated in water but not in hexane, a solvent composed of nonpolar molecules.

answer.solution: Crystals of NaCl dissolve in water, a polar liquid with a very large dipole moment, and the individual ions become strongly solvated. Hexane is a nonpolar liquid with a dipole moment of zero and, therefore, does not significantly interact with the ions of the NaCl crystals.

exercises.prompt: Explain why solutions of HBr in benzene (a nonpolar solvent) are nonconductive, while solutions in water (a polar solvent) are conductive.

answer.solution: A solution conducts only if it contains freely mobile, charged species. HBr, like HCl, is a covalent compound whose pure form contains no ions; it yields ions only by reacting with its solvent. Benzene is nonpolar and cannot accept an H<sup>+</sup> ion from HBr, nor could its molecules solvate the ions that would result, so HBr stays in benzene as neutral HBr molecules and the solution does not conduct. Water does accept the proton. HBr is a strong acid, and its reaction with water is essentially complete: $\text{HBr}(aq)+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}(l)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{\text{+}}(aq)+{\text{Br}}^{\text{−}}(aq)$. The polar water molecules surround and solvate the hydronium and bromide ions, which move freely through the solution and carry the current, so the aqueous solution is a good conductor.

exercises.prompt: Compare the processes that occur when methanol (CH<sub>3</sub>OH), hydrogen chloride (HCl), and sodium hydroxide (NaOH) dissolve in water. Write equations and prepare sketches showing the form in which each of these compounds is present in its respective solution.

answer.solution: Methanol is a covalent nonelectrolyte that neither ionizes nor reacts with water. Its molecules stay whole and disperse among the water molecules, held by hydrogen bonds between their O–H groups and water: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}(l)\;\longrightarrow \;\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}(aq)$. Hydrogen chloride is a covalent acid; its molecules react with water, transferring H<sup>+</sup> ions, and the reaction is essentially complete: $\text{HCl}(g)+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}(l)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{\text{+}}(aq)+{\text{Cl}}^{\text{−}}(aq)$. Sodium hydroxide is ionic, so it simply dissociates as water molecules surround and separate its ions: $\text{NaOH}(s)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{Na}}^{\text{+}}(aq)+{\text{OH}}^{\text{−}}(aq)$. The sketches show intact CH<sub>3</sub>OH molecules among water molecules for methanol; for HCl, H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> ions and no HCl molecules; and for NaOH, Na<sup>+</sup> and OH<sup>−</sup> ions. Around each cation the water molecules turn their partially negative oxygen ends inward, and around each anion their partially positive hydrogen ends.

exercises.prompt:
What is the expected electrical conductivity of the following solutions?
(a) NaOH(aq)
(b) HCl(aq)
(c) C6H12O6(aq) (glucose)
(d) NH3(aq)

answer.solution: (a) high conductivity (solute is an ionic compound that will dissociate when dissolved); (b) high conductivity (solute is a strong acid and will ionize completely when dissolved); (c) nonconductive (solute is a covalent compound, neither acid nor base, unreactive towards water); (d) low conductivity (solute is a weak base and will partially ionize when dissolved)

exercises.prompt: Why are most solid ionic compounds electrically nonconductive, whereas aqueous solutions of ionic compounds are good conductors? Would you expect a liquid (molten) ionic compound to be electrically conductive or nonconductive? Explain.

answer.solution: Electrical conduction requires charged species that are free to move. A solid ionic compound is made of ions, but the strong electrostatic attractions of the crystal hold each one in a fixed position, so the ions cannot migrate and the solid does not conduct. When the compound dissolves in water, it dissociates: water molecules surround and solvate the ions, reducing the forces between them, and the ions disperse and move freely through the solution, so the aqueous solution is a good conductor. A molten ionic compound is also expected to conduct. Melting frees the ions from their fixed positions in the crystal, and although they still attract one another, they can move past one another through the liquid and carry a current.
